utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to continue your portion of the final argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When we broke yesterday, I had just finished dealing with Counts 3 and 4. May I turn now to Counts 5 and 6, which allege the ill-treatment of Stanisa Radosevic and Novak Stijovic. The suggestion that these attacks were ethnically motivated was certainly not reflected in the treatment of Rosa Radosevic. At one point one of the men involved asked Stanisa Radosevic whether she was his mother. And when she said -- when he said that she was, the man replied, Then she is my mother too. Nor was there evidence of ethnically motivated violence in the treatment of Novak Stijovic's father Konstantin and his companions, who were apparently detained at about the same time. Taken as a whole, the evidence shows that four of the six Serb civilians who were detained at the Pozar crossroads on the 21st of April were released unharmed. And so too were other Serb civilians briefly detained elsewhere. It is, in our submission, clear that the men who ill-treated Mr. Radosevic and his companion picked on them because they believed that they were associated with the attack on Gllogjan. They were asked in terms about their associations with the MUP, and they were specifically asked who had been responsible for shooting at Albanian civilians on the 24th of March. Again, the Defence does not suggest that this excuses the violence, but it does contextualise it. The assaults were the acts of disorganized, ill-disciplined, and unauthorised village guards. They were carried out by unidentified men under no clear command. Both witnesses described the absence of organization and leadership among the groups that they encountered, and their testimony painted a picture of armed villagers taking to the streets with no defined or organized purpose. There is nothing to suggest that their actions were authorised or condoned in any way by Mr. Haradinaj or by any other person in authority. I want to turn now to the six Serb civilians from Ratishe and Dashinoc who were subsequently killed or went missing. The Prosecution makes the sweeping assertion that these people must have been murdered by members of the KLA, acting under orders. But there is, in fact, no reliable evidence of how these people died or who killed them. Counts 7 and 8 allege the murder of Vukosava Markovic and Darinka Kovac. The Chamber knows next to nothing about the circumstances of their disappearance, and their bodies were identified by so-called traditional means, a process which has resulted in a proven misidentification rate of 50 per cent on the facts of this case. Counts 9 and 10 allege the murder of Milovan and Milka Vlahovic. The only evidence as to the circumstances of their alleged abduction is an uncorroborated hearsay statement related by Miloica Vlahovic, their son. He testified that a man called Madjun Arifaj told him that his parents were taken away by uniformed armed men, but Arifaj didn't know who these men were. He provided no information about their appearance, their ethnicity, or the date of the incident, and surprisingly Miloica Vlahovic didn't ask him any of these questions. There's no corroboration and the Chamber has no means of assessing the reliability of the source. Vague and unsubstantiated testimony of this kind is of very little evidential value. In our submission, it can't properly form the basis of any reliable finding of fact. Counts 11 and 12 allege the murder of Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic. All of the available evidence points to the conclusion that these men sustained their fatal injuries in an exchange of fire. The Prosecution, though, is asking the Chamber to hold that these deaths involved the commission of a war crime without any reliable evidence whatsoever as to how this exchange of fire began or who fired the first shot. The Chamber has heard evidence that both men were members of the MUP reserve and that they bore a hostile intent towards the KLA. The evidence is at the very least consistent with the hypothesis that Slobodan Radosevic fired first, that fire was returned, and that both men were mortally injured in the resulting exchange. Beyond that, it is in our submission quite impossible to reach any reliable conclusions on the evidence. It is for the Prosecution to prove that these deaths involved the commission of war crimes, and the evidence falls far short of establishing this. Your Honours, no one doubts that these six people went missing from the villages of Dashinoc and Ratishe during the indictment period, but this doesn't begin to prove that they were unlawfully killed by members of the KLA, still less that they were murdered pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise involving Mr. Haradinaj. In addition to these six individuals, the indictment alleges the murder of a further six people of Serb ethnicity. The only direct evidence of any KLA involved in any of these cases relates to the alleged detention of Nenad Remistar in Jabllanice. I will deal with Jabllanice a little later in my submissions. As to the other five individuals, the Prosecution has adduced no reliable evidence at all as to the circumstances in which they met their deaths. Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic were armed members of the PJP and were on duty at the time of their disappearance. Both men were carrying automatic weapons, and they went missing shortly after they left the PJP contingent at the Baballoq refugee camp. There is no reliable evidence that they were kidnapped. The Prosecution has not proved that they were hors de combat at the time of their deaths. The evidence is entirely consistent with the hypothesis that they were killed in an exchange of fire. Ilija Antic was discovered missing from his home in Lloqan on the morning of the 29th of May. At the time of his disappearance, this was disputed territory and the VJ were planning a major offensive in the area which was due to begin on the very day he disappeared. There are any number of possible explanations for the death of Mr. Antic. Zdravko Radunovic went missing on the 16th of July somewhere between Gjakove and Dobric. The only evidence suggesting KLA involvement is derived from MUP interrogations of two KLA members called Krist and Leke Pervorfi. The Chamber excluded the statements signed by these men because there were strong grounds to doubt their reliability and voluntariness. Leke Pervorfi has alleged that he was tortured and the terrorism charges against both men were subsequently withdrawn. Any information emanating from those interrogations must be regarded as unreliable, and it is not in our submission open to the Prosecution to seek to re-introduce them by the back door through the testimony of Witness 68, who knew nothing at all about the conditions under which those interrogations took place. There is simply no reliable evidence as to the circumstances in which Zdravko Radunovic went missing or was killed. The same is true of Velizar Stosic and Ivan Zaric. Ivan Zaric was last seen heading for Grabanice on the 19th of May when the Serb attack on the village was imminent, and Velizar Stosic went missing in Loxha on the 17th of July, but there is no evidence at all as to who abducted or killed either of them or as to the circumstances in which they died. In an effort to shore up its case, the Prosecution alleges that the KLA targeted Serb civilian vehicles and mounted attacks on the Baballoq refugee camp. But the hard facts on the evidence are these: There is no evidence of a single civilian casualty arising from an alleged attack on a vehicle travelling along the main road. If it were true that these attacks were a regular occurrence, there would surely be some solid evidence of this fact. But the only direct evidence that the Prosecution has adduced relates to attacks on four armed police officers who were using civilian vehicles as a means of camouflage. The same picture emerges in relation to Baballoq. The Prosecution has not adduced evidence of a single civilian casualty. The only evidence of any attack on a civilian target was an account related to Witness 28 by two men she said she mistrusted. And she mistrusted them because they denied the presence of Serb police at a time when Albanians in the area were telling her that Serb forces were firing from inside the settlement itself. All of the hard evidence shows that the targets of KLA attacks during the indictment period were the Serbian PJP forces stationed in and around the settlement. Rade Repic testified that about a hundred of his men occupied the houses closest to the road, and the Trial Chamber has a series of contemporary records which show that every single reported attack was directed at members of the MUP. If the KLA had had a target -- a policy of targeting civilians at the refugee settlement, there would be at least some solid evidence of this. And finally, the Prosecution relies on generic evidence allegedly gathered and assimilated by the MUP and the RDB. The methods used to obtain much of this information included bribery, blackmail, and beating of detainees in police custody. Coming as it does from one of the protagonists to the conflict, we respectfully submit that unsourced and unparticularised generic assessments of this kind call for the greatest possible skepticism. In conclusion, we say that the allegation of a joint criminal enterprise to persecute, displace, and murder Serb civilians is completely unsupported by the evidence. I want to turn now to the alleged policy of persecution aimed at perceived collaborators and opponents. There is not the slightest evidence that Mr. Haradinaj ever authorised or condoned crimes of this kind. In fact, we say that the evidence points to the opposite conclusion. I want to group our submissions under four main heads. First, we submit that the investigation, detention, or questioning of suspected collaborators during an internal armed conflict in itself is lawful providing any detention is carried out humanely and in accordance with Common Article 3 and Additional Protocol II. It is not sufficient for the Prosecution to prove a policy of investigation or even detention. They must prove that there was a common criminal purpose to ill-treat suspected collaborators by torturing or summarily executing them. There is no evidence that Mr. Haradinaj ever did or said anything suggesting that he condoned that sort of behaviour, and that is our second submission. The only document issued in Mr. Haradinaj's name which even mentions collaborators is the set of military police regulations adopted on the 21st of June. But these regulations don't advocate mistreatment; they advocate investigation. They were adopted at a meeting in which Mr. Haradinaj spoke of the need to exclude criminal elements from the KLA. They expressly stipulate a requirement that only those of good character would be eligible for service with the military police, and they warn that anyone abusing their uniform would be stripped of their functions. This isn't evidence of a policy to ill-treat and summarily execute collaborators. Our third main submission is that the communiques issued in the name of the so-called General Staff between 1994 and 1997 do not reflect any policy on the part of Mr. Haradinaj. They were primarily propaganda tools, issued by unidentified members of the self-styled operational wing of the KLA, years before the situation in Kosovo escalated into open conflict. Indeed, it's a striking fact that none of the communiques claims responsibility for any attacks allegedly committed against collaborators in the indictment region or during the indictment period. No one knows who issued these communiques or who provided the information they contained. At least some of them contained bogus or exaggerated claims. Very few of the reported attacks on collaborators are corroborated, and in those few instances where there is some independent evidence, it relates to events occurring long before the indictment period and outside the indictment area. The Prosecution has completely failed to prove the nexus that it alleges. There's not the slightest evidence to suggest that Mr. Haradinaj ever provided any of the information contained in the communiques or approved of their content. In short, there is nothing whatsoever to suggest, much less to prove, that those documents reflected any policy on the part of Ramush Haradinaj. I want to move now to our fourth submission under this head. The mere fact that some individual members of the KLA may have ill-treated or killed suspected collaborators doesn't establish that they were acting under orders or pursuant to any common criminal purpose shared by Mr. Haradinaj. For the majority of victims of Albanian or Roma ethnicity, there is no evidence at all as to the identity of the perpetrators or the motive for the killings. Despite attempts by the Prosecution to twist and massage the facts of each of those cases into its overall case theory, there is direct evidence of suspected collaboration in only a small number of cases. The evidence shows that a total of seven victims named in the indictment were detained allegedly on grounds of suspected collaboration in two locations: Four of them in Jabllanice and three of them in Baran. The evidence does not suggest, much less prove, that Mr. Haradinaj authorised or condoned any of the ill-treatment which is alleged to have occurred at either of these locations. Indeed, we say that his interventions prove quite the opposite. The evidence shows that in every case where a disappearance or detention was reported to Mr. Haradinaj, he took action. The Prosecution characterizes his interventions as superficial, but it is, we say, important to keep clearly in mind that this is not a case in which command responsibility is alleged. The Prosecution alleges and the Prosecution must prove that these crimes were committed with Mr. Haradinaj's agreement, acquiescence, or approval, and it is against that allegation that his interventions fall to be judged. Let me start with Jabllanice. As the Chamber is by now well aware, Jabllanice had been a KLA stronghold for a number of years before the indictment period. After the 24th of March, it continued to operate independently. It was outside the area covered by the regional staff established in May, and it was not incorporated into any joint command structure until the 23rd of June. Mr. Haradinaj was never in day-to-day command at Jabllanice and there is no evidence to suggest that he was kept closely informed of the actions of those who were. Apart from his intervention on behalf of Skender Kuci, the evidence shows that he went to meetings in the staff headquarters on a total of three occasions during the indictment period. One of those meetings was attended by Bislim Zyrapi and other members of the General Staff. Mr. Zyrapi was late for the meeting because he'd been conducting an inspection of KLA positions in the village. He saw no signs of people being detained there. That is perhaps not surprising. Witness 6 testified that he was the only person held at Jabllanice for most of the time between the 13th of June and the 25th of July; and according to the dates he gave, he would almost certainly have been working in the kitchen by the middle of July when Zyrapi's visit took place. None of this evidence supports the proposition that the detention and alleged ill-treatment of suspects at Jabllanice would have been immediately obvious to any commander who attended a meeting in the staff headquarters in the centre of the village. Let me turn now to the case of Skender Kuci. The evidence shows that when Mr. Haradinaj was informed of his detention, he drove straight to Jabllanice with Rrustem Tetaj and ordered Nazmi Brahimaj to release him immediately. The Prosecution suggest that this is evidence of knowledge and acquiescence, but that is simply not right. When Nazmi Brahimaj said that Skender Kuci had been injured, Mr. Haradinaj issued an ultimatum. He said that nothing of the kind should ever happen again because it was damaging to the cause of the KLA. Those are not the words of a man who approved of what had happened. The plain fact is that there is no evidence that Mr. Haradinaj was ever made aware of the alleged ill-treatment of anyone else detained at Jabllanice, and there is no evidence that he ever entered the barracks area on the outskirts of the village. It's not enough for the Prosecution to make vague allegations that he must have known. Witness 6 testified that he never once saw Mr. Haradinaj at Jabllanice. In the final stage of his detention, during his period of relative freedom, Witness 6 was actively trying to find out the names of the main KLA figures involved and was able to see all of the movements into and out of the barracks enclosure. If Mr. Haradinaj had been in any way a party to the detention and alleged ill-treatment of the suspects held at Jabllanice, there would be at least some evidence of this in the Prosecution case but there's none. The evidence of Witness 3 underlines this. He said that when he was taken to Gllogjan by Lahi Brahimaj at the end of July, the commander who dealt with him there treated him well from the outset. He was given food to eat and asked whether he had relatives in Gllogjan he could spend the night with. When he said that he didn't, he was given a place to sleep and warned to keep away from the windows in case of a Serb attack. Shortly afterwards, he was told that arrangements had been made for him to return to his family, and after the intervention by the commander at Gllogjan he said that nothing ever happened to him again. In its closing brief, the Prosecution suggests that the commander at Gllogjan must have been Ramush Haradinaj. Well, if that's right, then it does nothing to support the Prosecution's case theory; on the contrary, it establishes that Mr. Haradinaj arranged for the immediate release of Witness 3, treated him humanely throughout, and organized his swift return to his family. Those are not the actions of a commander who approved of the ill-treatment of perceived collaborators and opponents. Just standing back for a moment, the position is this: There are four people who are on the evidence shown to have been accused of collaboration who were detained at Jabllanice. On the Prosecution's own case, out of those four Mr. Haradinaj intervened to secure the immediate release of two of them and a third has testified that he had nothing to do with his detention or alleged ill-treatment. Let me turn to Baran. During the first half of the indictment period, the Baran valley also operated independently. It too was outside the regional staff and was not incorporated into a joint command structure until the 23rd of June. Less than three weeks later, the village staffs in the Baran valley had ceased to exist and the KLA volunteers had relocated to the newly formed FARK barracks in Baran. Three of the victims named in the indictment were detained at Baran on various dates after the FARK barrack was established: Kemajl Gashi, Zenun Gashi, and Sanije Balaj. The evidence shows that Mete Krasniqi was directly involved in the detention of all three. He detained and interrogated Kemajl Gashi in his private office close to the FARK barracks, he ordered the arrest of Zenun Gashi, who was then taken to the FARK barracks by Vesel Dizdari, and he was instrumental in the initial detention of Sanije Balaj in full view of FARK soldiers immediately outside the FARK barracks. So it's necessary to focus in some detail on the role of Mete Krasniqi and his relationship with the officers under Witness 17's command. There is conflicting evidence as to whether Mete Krasniqi was a member of the military police unit that Witness 17 established on the 12th of July. Cufe Krasniqi, who helped to establish that unit, said that both Mete and Avni Krasniqi were members and were under the command of Hasan Gashi. To the extent that it's possible for the Chamber to rely on any of the evidence given by Avni Krasniqi, he too claimed that both he and his brother Mete were members of the FARK military police and that they operated under the command of Witness 17. But Rrustem Tetaj, who had been the subzone-commander or one of the subzone-commanders in the regional staff and Sadri Selca testified that Mete Krasniqi had not been formally appointed by anyone. A number of other witnesses described him as a self-styled or self-appointed commander. But whatever the formal position may have been, the evidence shows that Mete and Avni Krasniqi held themselves out as military police officers after the arrival of Witness 17. They were based in Baran and the evidence shows that they worked closely with FARK officers under Witness 17's command. In this context, Witness 17's self-serving attempts to distance himself from the actions of Mete Krasniqi and to suggest that there was some sort of parallel command structure in operation in Baran were hollow and unconvincing. It's worth just highlighting some of the key points. It was Witness 17 who permitted Mete Krasniqi to operate from an office within metres of his headquarters and who permitted him to enter the FARK barracks at will. It was Witness 17's deputy, Musa Dragaj, who took Medin Gashi to Mete Krasniqi's office when his father was detained there. It was Witness 17 who had notes relating to the interrogation of Kemajl and Medin Gashi in his own personal notebook. It was Witness 17 who personally authorised the detention and questioning of Sanije Balaj after she had been stopped by Mete and Avni Krasniqi immediately outside his barracks. And it was Witness 17 who had the name of Zenun Gashi recorded on the list of missing and wanted persons in his own personal notebook. His evidence about that list was evasive and defensive, but on one point he was clear: He never brought the existence of that list to the attention of Ramush Haradinaj. Taken as a whole, this evidence suggests a far closer degree of cooperation between Mete Krasniqi and the FARK brigade at Baran than Witness 17 was prepared to admit. By contrast, there is no evidence of any command relationship between Mete Krasniqi and Ramush Haradinaj. At its highest, the evidence shows that Mete Krasniqi was a rogue individual operating under no clear command, but he detained these three people right under the nose of Witness 17. If it was anyone's responsibility to ensure that crimes were not being committed in and around the FARK barracks during the second half of July and August, then it was Witness 17's. For him to come here and suggest that responsibility for Mete Krasniqi's actions should somehow be laid at the door of Ramush Haradinaj is to turn logic on its head. In this context, I want, if I may, to make three particular points about the abduction and murder of Sanije Balaj. The first point is that each of the Prosecution's main arguments ultimately depends on the credibility of Avni Krasniqi and his late brother Mete. Avni and Mete Krasniqi were the sole sources of the allegation that Idriz Gashi was intending to take Sanije Balaj to Gllogjan. The uncorroborated allegation that Idriz Balaj moved the body is also traceable directly back to Avni and Mete Krasniqi. For our part, we submit that the Trial Chamber cannot place any reliance on uncorroborated allegations made by Avni Krasniqi. It is, we suggest, quite clear that he deliberately and repeatedly lied about his own involvement in the detention and questioning of Sanije Balaj and about the involvement of his brother Mete and his cousin Iber. The evidence of Shaban Balaj, Witness 72, Vesel Dizdari, Cufe Krasniqi, and even Witness 17 all established beyond doubt that it was Mete and Avni Krasniqi who stopped and detained Sanije Balaj and that Avni and Iber Krasniqi were present and interfering during her interrogation. Avni Krasniqi's denials were patently untrue. Once it is clear that a witness has lied on matters as fundamental as this, the whole of his testimony must fall under suspicion. We submit that the credibility of Avni Krasniqi calls for the most anxious scrutiny. He was a prime suspect for the murder and has a previous conviction for a string of violent robberies. His account of his own involvement in the shooting was self-serving, unconvincing, and inconsistent with other evidence. For the reasons set out in our closing brief, we say that he had a powerful motive to lie, not only about his own involvement in the killing but also about who was responsible for the removal of the body. Secondly, we submit that there is no credible evidence that Idriz Gashi was a KLA commander or that he had been appointed to any position of responsibility by Ramush Haradinaj. The very fact that he had asked Witness 17 for a transfer to become one of his soldiers at the FARK barracks in Baran is inconsistent with the suggestion that he had a command responsibility elsewhere. But the transfer order signed by Ramush Haradinaj on the 7th of July puts the issue beyond doubt. It describes Idriz Gashi as "luftetari" or an ordinary soldier. It may well be that like Mete and Avni Krasniqi, he falsely held himself out to be some sort of commander; but there is clear and objective evidence that this was not, in fact, the truth. The third point I want to stress relates to the actions of Mr. Haradinaj. The evidence shows that he took a personal interest in the investigation into Sanije Balaj's death. He went with Gani Gjukaj to pay his condolences to the family, and even more significantly he personally confronted Mete Krasniqi in an effort to find out who had killed her. Within days, Fadil Nimonaj or Tigri had been allocated responsibility for investigating her disappearance. It is important to stress that this was a KLA investigation. Fadil Nimonaj was a member of the Dukagjini Plain Operational Staff and he had been appointed by Mr. Haradinaj as commander of the military police on the 25th of July. By the 21st of August, Mr. Haradinaj was based in Prapaqan himself, and it was there that the investigation office was set up. All of the relevant witnesses were interviewed, apart from Idriz Gashi who had by then absconded. The evidence shows that Mr. Haradinaj took part in at least one meeting with other commanders to discuss the progress of the investigation. But these are not the actions of a man who approved of what had happened. The Prosecution knows this, which is why it is driven to argue that all of this must have been some sort of elaborate sham, but there is not a scrap of evidence for that suggestion. Leaving aside the individuals detained at Jabllanice and Baran, there is, as I've said, no solid evidence that any of the other Albanian or Roma victims named in the indictment were targeted as suspected collaborators. I just want to take two particular examples. In the case of Nurije and Istref Krasniqi, the Prosecution points to rumours of collaboration, but there is an equally plausible alternative hypothesis: That they were abducted and killed as part of a long-running blood-feud with the family of Brahim and Avdi Krasniqi, a feud which had already claimed two lives and caused several critical and life-threatening injuries. A murder committed for private motives of revenge under the Kanun falls, we say, outside the joint criminal enterprise alleged on the indictment. It is immaterial that the perpetrators may have been members of the KLA. Indeed, there is evidence that the family of the victims were members of the KLA as well. As Rrustem Tetaj put it, these families were in a serious blood-feud and there was nothing to stop them killing each other. The suggestion that this couple was abducted on the orders of Rrustem Tetaj and taken to Gllogjan is based on the flimsiest possible evidence. It consists of uncorroborated, and quite possibly multiple, hearsay from questionable sources including the abductors themselves. It was denied by Mr. Tetaj and there is no reliable evidence to support it. But what the evidence does show is that Ramush Haradinaj undertook to make inquiries about the couple's disappearance and that Fadil Nimonaj was then appointed to conduct an investigation in this case as well. None of this is consistent with the allegation that Ramush Haradinaj was involved or approved of what had happened. Another illustration of the speculative nature of the Prosecution case theory is the shooting of Tush and Illira Frrokaj. There is no evidence at all to suggest that they were perceived to be collaborators or opponents of the KLA. At the time they went missing, there had been fighting in the area around Gllogjan, and according to Radovan Zlatkovic, there was a heavily armed Serb check-point in Irzniq. The forensic evidence suggests that the vehicle may well have been shot whilst the couple were travelling inside it. Bullet-holes to the vehicle itself and the presence of projectiles lodged in soft tissue lead to the inevitable conclusion, said Mr. Dunjic, that the velocity of the bullet had slowed. They could have been shot by anyone on either side for any reason. By the time Tush and Illira Frrokaj disappeared, Ramush Haradinaj had relocated to Prapaqan. In his absence, his brother Shkelzen responded to the inquiries of Witness 21 by asking for photographs of the couple, and saying that the KLA would look for them. Witness 21 testified that he was genuinely trying to help. None of that suggests that the KLA leadership in Gllogjan was in any way involved in the killing of this couple. Again, it suggests quite the opposite. The Prosecution has persisted in the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj permitted the KLA headquarters in Gllogjan to be used as a place for detention and torture of civilians, but there is no evidence of this whatsoever. Witness 17 said that he'd heard people using the expression "sent to Gllogjan," and that it was his belief that people who were sent to Gllogjan hardly ever came back. But under cross-examination it became clear that this was yet another instance in which he had made sweeping allegations in his 92 ter statement that he was unable to support with hard facts. It eventually came down to one conversation with an unidentified village commander, who provided no concrete information, and Witness 17 could not even identify the village that this person came from. Apart from the matters that I've already touched on, the only other evidence the Prosecution is able to point to is the detention of ECMM monitors Achilleas Pappas and Wolfgang Kaufmann and the ill-treatment of their interpreter, but the evidence shows that the conduct of Mr. Haradinaj towards that group was exemplary. Mr. Pappas said that Mr. Haradinaj questioned them gently and politely. He behaved calmly and reasonably towards them throughout, and organized an escort to ensure that they could leave the area safely. The assault on the interpreter was obviously quite wrong, but there is no suggestion that Mr. Haradinaj was present at the time or that any member of the ECMM team told him about it. There is, we say, nothing to suggest, still less to prove, that Mr. Haradinaj permitted that ill-treatment to occur. It's worth just recalling that the situation on the ground in Gllogjan and Irzniq on the day that this incident occurred is vividly portrayed in the BBC video which the Trial Chamber has seen on a number of occasions. The ECMM team had taken the very dangerous decision to drive directly into this offensive against Gllogjan in a Land Rover that resembled a Serb military vehicle a few days after the KLA had expressed public concern that interpreters travelling with internationals were misusing their freedom of movement to pass information on deployments and targets to the Serb forces. As Wolfgang Kaufmann said in his book, the men responsible for the assault on the interpreter had been under Serb fire for days; their nerves were shot and their fuses blew. He rightly recognised that Mr. Haradinaj got the ECMM team out of a very difficult situation. These are not the actions of a commander who approves of the ill-treatment alleged. I want to turn now to the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj established and maintained the Black Eagles as a means of intimidating the public and mistreating civilians. The evidence shows that the Black Eagles were established as a rapid reaction force. They were initially based in Gllogjan, and latterly in Irzniq, and would deploy to front line areas where the most intense fighting was taking place. But the Prosecution has not begun to prove that the Black Eagles engaged in any widespread pattern of crimes against civilians. They have adduced evidence alleging the personal involvement of Idriz Balaj in two pairs of counts on the indictment. As we make clear in our closing brief, we adopt Mr. Guy-Smith's submissions on the issue of identification, but whoever committed these crimes, there is not the slightest evidence that they were authorised by Mr. Haradinaj or that he condoned them or that he was even aware of them. Dealing first with Counts 13 and 14, Witness 4 testified that he'd never seen Ramush Haradinaj in Ratishe during the war, and all that he knew about him was that he was a good soldier and a good commander who neither killed nor imprisoned civilians. The evidence doesn't prove that these crimes were committed pursuant to any wider criminal purpose or agreement to which Mr. Haradinaj was a party; indeed for reasons more fully set out in our closing brief we submit that the motive for the alleged campaign against Witness 4's family remains entirely unclear. Turning to Counts 35 and 36, the Defence submits that there is no credibility evidence that the rape of Witness 61 was ever reported to Ramush Haradinaj. The statements of Witness 1 on this issue are internally inconsistent, uncorroborated, and inconsistent with other evidence in the case. Having regard to the Chamber's decision under Rule 92 quater, the Defence submits that no finding of fact could properly be based on this uncorroborated allegation. Indeed, we note that the Prosecution has adopted it neither in its closing brief nor in its oral submissions. The Prosecution does, however, rely -- the Prosecution does, however, rely on a number of other occasions on which it alleges that complaints were made to Ramush Haradinaj about the conduct of Idriz Balaj. None of those instances stands up to serious scrutiny as an allegation that Mr. Haradinaj failed to prevent or punish the commission of war crimes. First, the Prosecution relies on an alleged shooting incident in Irzniq in which a man called Adem Hulaj was injured. This incident is not included in the indictment and the Trial Chamber has heard no direct evidence about it. But the hearsay evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard is to the effect that the shooting was accidental. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, there is no basis whatever to conclude that Mr. Haradinaj failed to deal with the incident in a manner which was appropriate to the circumstances. Second, the Prosecution relies on the evidence of Witness 17 that he reported an incident of insubordination to Mr. Haradinaj. This incident occurred in Irzniq in July, when Mr. Balaj allegedly challenged Witness 17 to show his identification, and Witness 17 responded by producing an automatic weapon and saying that was all the authorisation he needed. We say that there was no basis at all for taking disciplinary action against Idriz Balaj over this incident; on the contrary, it was Witness 17 who had reacted aggressively to what he perceived as a challenge to his authority. In any event, this trivial incident does not constitute anything approaching a crime. Thirdly, the Prosecution relies on the allegation that during the reorganization of the zone command on or about the 21st of August, Witness 17 and Tahir Zemaj warned Mr. Haradinaj that Idriz Balaj was committing crimes against civilians. But again, as so often was the case, under cross-examination this was unsupported by hard facts. Witness 17 admitted that neither he nor Tahir Zemaj had communicated any specific or concrete allegation to Mr. Haradinaj which could have been investigated or which could have led to disciplinary action. They were merely repeating generalised rumour. The suggestion that Mr. Haradinaj responded with indifference to this report is also completely unjustified. He responded in the only way that any commander could respond to unparticularised rumours about one of his men. He said that he would look into them. This conversation took place towards the very end of the indictment period, at a time when Mr. Haradinaj had surrendered his command to Tahir Zemaj. It does not provide any support for the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj tolerated the commission of crimes against civilians. I'm going to move now to the third section of my submissions. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber, given that the interpreters are obviously working quite hard, would like to take the break at this stage or would like to continue for a further period of time. I'm very happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- following the speed. If you would try and keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- by the way, is it true that you gave a written copy of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I notice now and then, especially if the translation is a bit behind, that sometimes I hear small elements which do not change what you say, but apparently, for example, one of the things I noticed that something about the disciplinary action against Mr. Balaj, the name was repeated. utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I then turn to the third main part of our submissions, the finding of human remains in the vicinity of the Lake Radoniq canal and the inferences which can properly be drawn from this evidence. Put shortly, we say that the evidence does not establish that the canal was an execution site, nor does it establish that it was a dumping-ground in territory exclusively controlled by the KLA. The mere fact that the remains of a particular person were found in or around the canal cannot lead to an inference that the individual concerned was killed by members of the KLA pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise. We make eight main submissions in relation to this part of the Prosecution case. First, we make the rather obvious submission that each of these individuals disappeared or died in different parts of the indictment region, at different times during the indictment period. No one suggests that these findings are evidence that these people all died in the same incident. Many of the deaths occurred in circumstances which remain entirely unclear, and there is no solid evidence of any connection between them. An important key to unlocking the Prosecution's case theory is the position which they take in relation to the five unidentified sets of remains. The Prosecution is asking the Trial Chamber to say that they have proved beyond reasonable doubt that those five people were killed by the KLA for a purpose connected with the alleged joint criminal enterprise on the basis that their deaths fall into some pattern. But the Prosecution has no idea who these people were, what their ethnicity was, where they came from, where or when they died, or who killed them. The only thing they have in common is that they were found at the canal. This is a criminal trial not an exercise in speculative hypothesis. But the reason I say these individuals are important is because that's where the Prosecution's case theory starts to unravel, because they're taking essentially the same approach for the majority of these bodies. The mere fact that there is evidence of a person's name or evidence of the place where they were last seen alive makes no difference if there's no evidence as to who killed them or why. That's why I said at the outset that it is essential to examine the evidence on each count individually, and that's why Mr. Re tried to steer the Trial Chamber's analysis in the opposite direction. Secondly, we submit that there is no evidence as to when or how these bodies came to be in the positions in which they were found. As regards the bodies found in the natural section of the canyon, the evidence shows that they were almost certainly washed into the position in which they were found by the exceptionally heavy current that flushed through the canal during 1998. They could have entered the water at any point between the gates at Lluka e Eperme and the positions in which they were found. And there is unequivocal evidence that Serb ground forces were stationed in the vicinity of Lluka e Eperme from early May at the latest. In respect of the bodies found next to the canal wall, the Chamber is faced with a conflict of expert evidence as to how long they had been there. Professor Lecomte was of the view that it was more likely than not that the bodies had been moved into position shortly before they were found. Professor Aleksandric was of the opinion that at least some of the bodies had probably been killed there, but he based his opinion solely on the fact that there was projectile damage to the canal walls. I'll come back to the significance of the projectile damage in a while. But in the end, none of the experts could say with any degree of certainty, and certainly not with the degree of certainty required in a criminal trial, which, if any, of the bodies had been killed at the site or how or when they got there. Professor Aleksandric agreed that it was impossible to say for certain that any particular individual had been shot at the canal, and he agreed that any attempt to distinguish between them for that purpose would ultimately be a matter of speculation. Whether taken separately or together, the expert evidence cannot prove that any particular one of these individuals was executed at the canal. Leaving the expert evidence aside for a moment, the testimony of Witness 21 strongly suggests that at least some bodies were moved shortly before the arrival of the Serb forensic team. He visited the area twice, and allowing the greatest possible latitude those visits took place in the last week of August or the first week of September. He claimed to have seen the bodies of a child and several adult males inside the troughs of one of the cow-sheds at the economic farm. If his evidence on this is reliable, then those bodies had certainly been moved between the date of his visit and the arrival of the Serb forensic team. More significantly, he crossed the canal in both directions on two separate occasions, very close to the location where the bodies were subsequently found. He identified the two bodies shown in the photograph floating in the concrete section of the canal which were adjacent to where the other bodies were subsequently found. But despite the fact that the very purpose of his visit was to look actively for human remains, he didn't see any bodies by the wall or the ground by the wall adjacent to the canal on either of his visits. Our third submission is that the Prosecution's total area of control theory is a myth. Serb forces were present and operating in this area throughout the indictment period, and there is direct evidence from Serb officials that at various times those forces took part in armed engagements in the very position where the bodies were found. Time doesn't permit a thorough review of the evidence, but I do just want to highlight a few key points. Branko Gajic, head of VJ intelligence, testified that from the beginning of the indictment period Serb forces were stationed in a horseshoe formation around the lake, acting as a bone in the throat of the terrorists. But importantly, he said that these forces included a forward position at ground level at the base of Suka Radoniq. Dragan Zivanovic, commander of the 125th Brigade, testified that the Serb forces in this area engaged in what he called mobile camping, which involved conducting exercises in the field. The distances involved are not great. As Colonel Crosland pointed out, it would be very surprising indeed if Serb forces on the ground had not conducted operations in this area; this, after all, was a potential retreat route for the KLA. And as Mr. Re reminded us yesterday, Colonel Crosland also testified that Serb forces would conduct operations as far as 5 or 6 kilometres into the territory east of the main road. But the evidence is more specific than that. Zarko Bajcetic, the assistant head of the RDB in Gjakove, testified that from the time of his arrival at the beginning of July there were frequent clashes between Serb forces and the KLA in the area, some of which took place around the end of the concrete section of the canal. He was asked directly whether, to his knowledge, there had been armed clashes in the specific area where the bodies were ultimately found, and he confirmed that there had. His evidence on this could not have been clearer. Equally, there can be no doubt that Serb forces were all over the canal area during the August offensive against Gllogjan. Colonel Zivanovic drew a map of this offensive, from which it is clear that PJP forces were conducting operations at the economic farm and at the canal itself. He drew an arrow which cuts right across the territory around the economic farm, and these PJP forces weren't just passing through, they engaged in close combat. Shemsedin Cekaj said that a KLA soldier was killed at the canal at this time. The canal of course passes directly through Irzniq, and as I've already mentioned, Radovan Zlatkovic testified that there was a heavily armed Serb check-point continuously situated at Irzniq from the 12th of August onwards. And Witness 21 saw a Serb tank on the Ratishe side of the canal at the time of his second visit to the area. The Prosecution has clung on to the theory that Serb forces did not operate on the ground in this area, but the evidence clearly shows that they did. Our fourth submission leads on from the third. The fact that there was projectile damage to the canal walls and that ammunition of Chinese manufacture was found in the vicinity proves nothing. Once it's accepted that armed engagements took place in the very area where the bodies were found, the significance of this evidence disappears. Can I just draw attention to three matters in particular under this heading. First, there was projectile damage to both canal walls, going in opposite directions, which is entirely consistent with an exchange of fire across the canal. Secondly, there is no forensic evidence to connect the projectile damage on the walls with any of the projectiles recovered from the human remains found in the vicinity. And thirdly, there is documentary evidence showing that a few months after the end of the indictment period PJP forces operating out of Gjakove were being issued with a set of Chinese ammunition, in addition to their normal regular ammunition sets, in what can only have been an attempt falsely to implicate the KLA. Prosecution alleges that the canal was a KLA execution site, and it's for the Prosecution to prove this. They have completely failed, in our submission, to discharge that burden. Our fifth submission relates to the bodies discovered at the economic farm. The evidence shows that these individuals disappeared between the 30th of August and the 6th of September. The post mortem evidence is consistent with those dates. The Prosecution has never sought to explain why it removed those individuals from the indictment, but in our submission the reason is obvious. These people died at the time of the Serb September offensive. But one of those bodies, RE-1, was recovered by the Serb forensic team on the 11th of September before any of the other bodies were recovered. We say that the removal of RE-1 from the indictment is a clear concession - and a correct one - that the central thrust of the Prosecution's case theory is flawed. The mere fact that remains were found in this area can't prove that they were killed by the KLA. As to the remainder of the RE bodies, the expert evidence of Professor Lecomte is that they had been dead for between eight and 15 days at the time of their discovery on the 23rd of September. Well, if that's right, then it would mean that they were killed and placed into the positions in which they were found between the 8th and the 15th of September, at a time when this area was fully under Serbian military control. Now, the Prosecution suggests that the economic farm bodies are irrelevant because they have been removed from the indictment, but in our submission they are clearly not irrelevant. They raise the real possibility that the bodies of people killed in the Serb September offensive were dumped at the economic farm in an attempt to implicate the KLA. Our sixth submission relates to the two bodies that disappeared from the concrete section of the canal at some point between the 8th and the 11th of September, and I can take this shortly. In its closing brief, the Prosecution accepts that these bodies were never recovered by the Serb forensic team and seeks to suggest that they must have been washed along the entire length of the canyon and swept into the lake itself. That submission is inconsistent with the report of the specialist MUP diving team who examined the canyon and ruled out the possibility that bodies could have washed into the lake, an assessment which Professor Aleksandric who was there on the ground accepted as correct. If those two bodies were not washed into the lake, then the question which arises is: What happened to them? At the very least, it suggests that the integrity of the crime scene may have been compromised, but it is equally consistent with the hypothesis that they were removed because somebody in the operation knew that they could be identified as victims of crimes committed by Serb forces. It would certainly not be the only time that Serb forces had engaged in the removal of bodies to cover up the commission of war crimes. And the presence of Vlastimir Djordjevic in the initial reconnaissance party is an ever-present reminder of the need for special caution in evaluating the integrity of this investigation. Our seventh submission relates to the statements allegedly made by Bekim Kalamashi, Zenel Alija, and Lujlj Musaj during their interrogations by the MUP and the RDB. We suggest that these statements were nothing more than a pretext for the discovery of the canal. There is credible evidence before the Trial Chamber suggesting that they were obtained as a result of ill-treatment, allegations that were first made during the trial of Zenel Alija and Bekim Kalamashi in January 2000, and there are points of detail in the evidence of the Serb police witnesses which give credence to these allegations. But there are also serious and unexplained anomalies with the statements themselves. We suggest, and suggest clearly, that a review of the transcript leads to the inevitable conclusion that the testimony the Chamber received in an effort to explain these anomalies away from Radovan Zlatkovic, Bogdan Tomas, and others was patently untrue. Even the public prosecutor, Zoran Babic, who attended the canal on the 10th of September, and who would have been provided with the complete case file from the MUP interrogations, recorded in an official document to the Pec district court on the 9th that Zenel Alija and Bekim Kalamashi were at liberty, when in fact they'd been in MUP custody for nearly a week. I don't propose to go through all the details in my oral submissions; they are fully set out in our closing brief. But we do say that the falsification and backdating of documents, the pretense that people were at liberty when they were in custody, and the unexplained insertion of additional text into statements all point to one conclusion: That this aspect of the investigation was a sham. The obvious inference is that these men had words put into their mouths and were beaten into signing statements which had been written for them. It's all consistent, in our submission, with the other anomalies, and raises the real spectre that MUP personnel were engaged in a concerted fabrication of evidence, and one doesn't have to look far to see the reason. There's no doubt that the discovery of the canal was a propaganda coup for the Serbs, and the officials on the ground were inexplicably fast in exploiting that. Within hours of the supposed discovery, journalists, international observers, and even senior Serb politicians from Belgrade were at the scene. Most surprising aspect of this is that they arrived at the canal before its discovery had even been reported to Zarko Bajcetic, the man who sent the reconnaissance party. No one could provide any explanation for this, and Mr. Bajcetic confirmed that the reconnaissance team were incommunicado because there was no radio or telephone coverage in the area. I see the time. I'm going to move on to one or two topics towards the end. I've got about five or ten minutes to go. I'm happy to break at this stage or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do it in seven minutes, then perhaps it's best to finish it now --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I can do it in seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we have a more natural point where we have a break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Our eighth and final submission concerning the canal relates to the ballistics evidence. For reasons which are set out in our closing brief, we submit that the Prosecution has not proved that the cartridges found at the canal were linked to cartridge cases allegedly recovered in Gllogjan on the 24th of March. Neither the opinion evidence of Milutin Visnjic, nor the testimony of Nebojsa Avramovic establishes the nexus the Prosecution alleges. There can be no justification for reading into the ballistics report words which flatly contradict what it says. And even if there were, the likelihood that weapons were circulating and the undisputed evidence that there had been armed engagements in the area of the canal provides a complete explanation for the presence of cartridge casings in that vicinity. Before I leave the subject of the canal, I just want to say a final word about Witness 17's account of the meeting on the 21st of August at Prapaqan and his claim that one of those present had made a remark about the fish in Lake Radoniq getting fat on human flesh. We say that in this, as in so many other aspects of his testimony, there are serious grounds to doubt his reliability. He made no remark -- no note, I'm sorry, no note of the remark in his personal notes of the meeting, and the claim that it was met with silence was effectively withdrawn in answer to a direct question from the Trial Chamber when he said he could not remember one way or the other whether there had been an objection or response. Nor has the Prosecution established any independent corroboration for his testimony about this meeting. Although Zoran Stijovic said that this remark was reported to the RDB, he was unable to exclude the possibility that Witness 17 was the source of the RDB's information. He said that the remark had been reported by only one of the RDB's sources at the meeting, and he confirmed that those sources included members of the FARK. May I turn briefly before I conclude to the law. All of our submissions are set out in full in our closing brief. I'm going to deal with them very briefly indeed. We say that the counts alleging crimes against humanity are unfounded; the crimes alleged, even if proved, do not amount to a widespread or systematic attack on the Serb civilian population. They're not on such a scale or such a frequency or intensity as to constitute an attack on a civilian population as such. Nor can it be said that the individuals of Albanian or Roma ethnicity named in the indictment are sufficiently numerous to constitute a civilian population for this purpose. They were very limited in number compared to the civilian population as a whole, and it can't be said that the civilian population itself was the subject of an attack or that perceived collaborators were of a class or category so numerous that they themselves constituted a civilian population. And we adopt and urge upon you the analysis of the Trial Chamber in Limaj. So far as armed conflict is concerned, we say the evidence shows that the end of May had marked a watershed when a series of intermittent and sporadic armed engagements spilled over into full-scale armed conflict for the reasons we have set out. In conclusion, then, we submit that the Prosecution has failed to prove the existence of the joint criminal enterprise alleged on the indictment, the Prosecution has failed to prove Mr. Haradinaj's personal participation in any of the crimes alleged, the Prosecution has failed to prove that he ordered, authorised, or condoned any of these crimes, and none of the allegations concerning his alleged contribution to the joint criminal enterprise have been proved. We submit he's entitled to be acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a little bit over two hours. That means that approximately -- a little bit less than two and a half hours would remain for the other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what we understand we have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And will you take both more or less an equal share of that time or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We will share and share alike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that means --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the Chamber may be asking a slightly different question which is: Will both of us finish in time to proceed with any further arguments on any other issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had in mind, as a matter of fact, that the close to two hours remaining that that would take approximately the remainder of the day, and I was just wondering whether the next break would be after you had finished or after Mr. Harvey is finished, dependent on who starts after the break or whether part of one of your submissions you would have to consider to have a little bit longer first session and then a shorter second one. Then of course I was also concerned whether that would be suitable for the interpreters, technicians, and transcribers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that most probably I will be going -- not most probably, I will be going next and most probably I will finish at/or shortly before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
