utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, first of all, the apologies of the Chamber for the late start. There were reasons why we were delayed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One golden thread. One golden thread is always to be seen in the temple of justice, and that is the duty of the Prosecution to prove the accused's guilt subject to what it has undertaken to prove beyond a reasonable doubt. It is to the evidence introduced at trial and to it alone that a finder of fact, and here you, this Chamber, are to look for for that proof. No conjecture, assumption, innuendo, or speculation. A reasonable doubt as to the guilt of any of the accused may arise from the evidence, conflict in the evidence, or the lack of evidence. The Prosecution has failed to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt. You should find each of the accused not guilty, and we submit that in this case that would be an appropriate finding. I wish to backtrack for a moment and take a look at some of the things -- or really one thing that happened during the course of the trial, and that was during the examination of a particular witness when the issue of apartheid came up and the Prosecution objected to the use of the term, "apartheid," the policy or practice of political, legal, economic, or social discrimination. And the reason that I raise it now is because in the introduction to the Prosecution's brief and in the comments made by Mr. Re yesterday, he indicated that the Serb authorities were engaging in increasingly, the next word, legal repressive means, as if those who would fight against, protest against, or otherwise complain against legally repressive means are at fault. And indeed, if we take a look at the evidence and the testimony of many witnesses who came from one side, we will find that that indeed was their attitude about those that fought against them. In reviewing for but a moment the notion of legally repressive means, I'm reminded of what I was talking about before, which is the apartheid legislation in South Africa, the 1940s, the 1950s, the 1960s, the 1970s, the Vichy laws, the Nuremberg laws, and for a moment I'll comment on the May laws of 1882, when Tsar Alexander III banned Jews from areas and set quotas on higher education, quotas as to how many young men or women could attend school. And the reason that I mentioned that, quite specifically, on a personal level is because my great grandfather was beaten to death because he refused to give up the quota for my grandfather. And my grandfather and the rest of the family after that left Russia. To use such a term as "legally repressive means" in this forum and give it any basis of credibility is extremely troublesome. What was the reality here? What happened? A small group of people attempted to bring their communities together to fight to free themselves from the legally repressive laws; to get weapons to fight to free themselves from the legally repressive laws; to get uniforms and supplies to fight to free themselves from the legally repressive laws; to attempt to organize an army to fight to free themselves from the legally repressive laws; to set up hospitals to care for the wounded and dying who had fought to fight -- were in their fight to free themselves from legally repressive laws. You've heard evidence here that after what occurred in Prekaz, Likoshan, and Gllogjan there was a grand swell of support. There's no reason in such a situation to intimidate people who were already supporting you. There's no reason to do so, though as the Prosecution has stated in the fourth amended indictment, to consolidate control over the Dukagjin Zone because do recall, please, that that is what is considered to be and what is identified as being the common criminal purpose. That common criminal purpose has changed in the argument made yesterday and I'll speak about that in a moment. The Prosecution position in this case is, in our submission, intellectually and, at times, factually inaccurate at best. They have avoided the reality of what was occurring on the ground in the region and to the people living there. They have compartmentalized their case when convenient and generalised when convenient. They have engaged in a number of unsubstantiated assertions; in fact, the Prosecution in this case has been a moving target, the goal-posts have moved depending on what is most advantageous to their case or what they believe they should go for next, as opposed to what the evidence they have adduced is and what it proves. When given the opportunity to confront their own witnesses - and I say that again, their own witnesses, because each and every witness in this case was brought to you by the Prosecution, each and every witness was either spoken to by an investigator and/or proofed prior to testifying. In that context, when given the opportunity to confront their witnesses with contradictions or differences from that which they testified to on a number of occasions, and important ones, they have avoided obtaining the information whilst that witness is testifying viva voce and under oath, instead on occasion they have attempted to impeach or discredit such testimony after it's all over. It's a form of cherry-picking retroactively, and an example of that most assuredly is a discussion of when the Black Eagles were formed and the evidence of Ylber Haskaj in that regard which I will get to further on. One of the things that's occurred here, and it's important because all parties I believe should recognise that the Kosovo Liberation Army was a nascent group at best struggling to put together an effective fighting force, and we have been engaged in the activity of attempting to fit a square peg into a round hole. The best example of is that is when they discuss what occurs in a normal military in paragraph 172 of their brief. The KLA was comprised of young men, men in their 20s, without great experience, if any experience, in what some call the art and others call the horror of war. This was not a normal military. What's at stake in this case, apart from what's at stake in every case where there is a criminal matter? Part of what's at stake in this case is, I suggest to you, the integrity of a system. You gentlemen cannot convict when the core of the Prosecution's case is built on unproven assumption and conjecture, reliance on rumour, unreliable testimony, unreliable forensic evidence, manufactured and fabricated evidence, at times orchestrated as we've heard clearly by the MUP, obtained forged or obtained -- forged or obtained from young men beaten or tortured information. It is, and I put this most simply, a cancer at the heart of this case, and it's what this evidence shows when you go through it patiently, when you go through it carefully, when you go through it scientifically, logically, methodically, that's what it shows. And you cannot convict on that evidence, we submit. There are many, many reasonable doubts buried right in the heart of this case, and they have been demonstrated to you. We do not have to prove them, but the evidence have shown. In Mr. Re's opening statement and also in his closing remarks, he has said that because bodies were found by the concrete wall, that proves that it's an execution site. At the beginning of the case, he said, including other things, that - and this is at 403 - because body R-1 was found near the wall, that proves this was an execution site. Well, when he made the comment to you then, and similarly when he has made the comments that he's made to you yesterday, he has engaged in an old logical fallacy: Post hoc ergo propter hoc, after this, therefore because of this. And this fallacy is based on the mistaken notion that simply because one thing happens after another, the first event was the cause of the second event. This reasoning has been recognised as the basis for many erroneous beliefs and has been recognised as the basis for many failures of proof. In addition, there have been what we submit are misstatements, material misstatements, in the record of which I will give you two examples. Mr. Balaj was already a prominent figure, referring to the assertion that he was seen on March -- sometime after March 24th at a funeral in Gllogjan, paragraph 237. This claim finds no support in the evidence. This claim comes from Witness 1. It is asserted to come from an unnamed, unknown, unsourced Albanian villager who Witness 1 claimed pointed Idriz Balaj out at a funeral. It is untested, and they have from this one piece of what we submit is unreliable information generalised to a non-existent assertion of proof that of common knowledge that he was a prominent figure. Another example may be found at paragraph 482, where they attribute to him being involved in an execution based on evidence that was never admitted. I want to turn for a moment to a couple of issues because they need a bit of attention, and then I will place the balance of my remarks to the specific -- some specific counts. It has been suggested that Idriz Balaj intimidated Witness 17. This is the intimidation that Witness 17 suffered we found at page 7572 and 7573 of the transcript. "Initially I tried to consider it as a joke," starting at line 22, "but when he insisted that I reacted and I asked him whether he knew me, who I was, he said, No, I don't know you. Then I showed him an automatic weapon and a few hand-grenades and I told him that I was a commander of a brigade and nobody could stop me from going to the military hospital to visit a friend, and that is why I asked Ramush to either dismiss him or to discipline him because incidents like these could lead to greater consequences." That's not intimidation; that's a professional military man taking umbrage at some young upstart in his view challenging his authority. The Prosecution also has discussed the beating of an interpreter, and an examination of the record in that regard - and I certainly don't condone the beating of anyone - an interpreter taller than Idriz Balaj, he is hitting him, kicking him, and his nerves are shot. He is concerned that something may be amiss, and the incident is resolved without much further ado. They were stopped in a war zone during a particularly horrific time for members of the KLA, during a period of time when they were suffering one of the major onslaughts by the Serbian forces. Going through not only the Prosecution's brief but also listening to the remarks made yesterday, I think that it's not unfair to say that they are attempting to establish Idriz Balaj's guilt based on bad character, based on rumour, gossip; but that does not substitute for evidence nor in any fashion prove his culpability or his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. In attempting to rely on this kind of evidence, rumours of his misconduct, they do at least three improper things: They violate the fundamental rule of fairness in contravention of Article 21 that prohibits the use of such testimony; they, as I said, attempt to establish the guilt of Mr. Balaj by hearsay gossip and not through testimony that is trustworthy and inherently believable; and thirdly, they leave him so painted with no means of defending himself. For what is rumour but a cruel story on wheels and every hand oils those wheels as they run. It's like a virus. It has a viral nature that spins out of control. It's been said about rumour over the years, enemies carry a report different in form than the original, but one invents the rest in large. Rumour opens a veritable Pandora's box of irresponsible gossip, innuendo, and smear. It is not relevant evidence in any respect to prove a particular fact nor is it reliable testimony as to remarks and stories of unidentified people constituting generalised hearsay and gossip. It was said in this court at one point by the Chamber, at 1007: "If you have no further information about the source of these rumours, then I would invite you," leaving the name out, "to move on to your next subject," because you understand in a court of law, which is where we are, in a court of law, not in a coffee shop, not in a bar, not sitting at a table where any kind of remarks can be made. Rumours in a court of law can play only a very limited role at all. Questions have been asked, statements have been made, He was the most notorious, he was the most brutal, and no facts to support these. As a matter of fact, when asked again and again, Witness 17 had no information, Mr. Tetaj said, Oh, yes, when he comes the people love him. If there's been a Serb attack, because what does he do? He protects the people. But when the Serbs are not there, the people fear him and his presence because the knowledge that he is present in the area can bring by and bring back to the village the very thing that they are so concerned about, which is war. His job was to command a special rapid intervention unit to go where he was needed, to fight in those battles, to train young men to give their lives to fight against the legally repressive means brought upon them by the Serbian authorities. Finally, in terms of dealing with the issue of rumour, it has been said in more than one culture that trying to squash a rumour is like trying to catch the wind or water with a net. And rumour, gossip, without a leg to stand on will get around some other way. I suggest to you that in viewing the evidence as it relates to Idriz Balaj, you pay particular attention to the extent to which you're being invited to damn him for a reputation as opposed to analyse the actual facts that exist. I'm now going to discuss specifically Counts 13 and 14, counts in which there has been an allegation that Mr. Balaj was personally involved. Criminal trial is, among other things, an attempt to reconstruct the past event to aid the trier of fact in determining what happened. Physical trace evidence, such as finger-prints, fibres, or blood are often used to assist this reconstruction, because when they are properly collected and analysed, trace evidence can help determine the nature of the events and the identity of the perpetrator. Eye-witness evidence can be likened to another form of trace evidence, in effect it is a criminal event involving an eye-witness, leaves a trace in the brain of the eye-witness; the memory as trace evidence has rich implications. Like physical evidence, memory trace evidence can be contaminated, lost, destroyed, or otherwise made to produce results that can lead to an incorrect reconstruction of the event in question. Like physical trace evidence, the manner in which memory trace evidence is collected can have important consequences for the accuracy of those results. When dealing with memory, it is well acknowledged and recognised that nothing tends to obscure the memory so much as the lapse of time, and nothing can be as dangerous as relying on such memory which has been objectively shown to potentially have been influenced by factors that have altered the reality of what happened. This is particularly true where the facts testified to occurred in the early youth of a witness. Such testimony is unsafe to act upon except so far that it is borne out by those facts which have been objectively proven. There's a famous study which I'm sure the Chamber's aware of, as the Chamber has indicated it has a fair, if not comprehensive appreciation of the area of eye-witness identification, it's the "lost in the mall" study, where young people -- well, maybe actually not so young, they were college students and even older, were asked whether or not they had ever been lost in a mall and they said, No, it didn't happen. Then they received information from other people who they seemingly would have trusted such as professors or mothers or fathers or uncles who related such an incident where they had been lost in a mall. Over 25 per cent of the subjects who initially completely denied such an event, after having the most elementary of suggestions, completely agreed that they participated in an event that never took place with people who were not there. Now, I dwell on these considerations at the outset, because as the Chamber is aware the most common cause of wrongful convictions is eye-witness misidentification. This is not news. This is something that anyone who was involved in the business of law, police, prosecutor, defence attorney, judge knows about. This information has been known since 1932 in a book by Professor Edwin Borchard. In later studies that have been done and specifically a study that was done in the United States where much of this work has been vigorously pursued, dealing with exonerations, in 64 per cent of the cases that have been exonerated between the years of 1989 through 2003, at least one eye-witness misidentified the defendant. In almost 90 per cent of the rape cases there has been a misidentification. Now, why is that important in this case? Pretty obvious reasons. In order to understand what occurred in the minds of - and I'm going to start with - Witness 4, I note for purposes of this discussion that there has been no mention of Witness 19. It is my assumption that the Prosecution concedes that he made no identification at all. If we use the following time-line for the moment and some objective facts, this is what we find to be true. Slobodan Praskevic was shot on March 2nd. The mother returns two weeks later, March 16th. The first visit to the house is March 30th, two weeks later, according to the testimony of Witness 4. Now, the first visit to the house is a visit where there are people in black. Witness 4 very clearly makes it known that he does not see anybody, let alone the individual that he identifies as Toger on the 30th. There is an illusion that by March 30th, because they're the special unit of the night, that the special unit of the night must be the Black Eagles, but we have information from Ylber Haskaj that the Black Eagles were not formed until May 14th. One to two weeks later, so it's between April 7th and April 14th, Sister S who has been taken on the first night returns. At that time, according to the information that we have, Witness 4 could not have seen her because -- I'm sorry, could not have seen him and recognised him because he was at a distance of 50 to 60 metres away by a car or in a car. The third time, the third sighting of what the Prosecution claims is Toger is a week to two afterwards, where once again he does not see the individual who he claims to be Idriz Balaj. Now, what happens, and which is very, very important in a place where you do need to really look at his testimony is when the individual returns after he has dropped Sister S off and has returned to his home some 40 minutes after that has occurred, he testified that two people came up in a car and when asked who were these people, what were they wearing, he said, Well, I recognise one of them, the same person I've seen all the times before. But that's impossible, it couldn't have happened. He didn't see him. So what happened here? What is going on with this young man's memory? And I please, I call him not a liar, but I do call him mistaken. And I suggest to you the Chamber's well aware of what occurred. His memory was infected. By what? By seeing Idriz Balaj on television, by seeing the name "Toger" attributed to Idriz Balaj on television, not only in a notorious case did this occur but it also occurred when there was an attempted assassination on his life. This young man wishes to resolve his pain, and I understand that. He wishes to resolve his case and he wishes to attribute some responsibility to someone, but based on the evidence that's before this Chamber I suggest to you that that's not safe or reliable. You could rely on - and it's been suggested - some circumstantial evidence perhaps. What would that be? Black uniforms. Who in this case did not wear a black uniform? Villagers wore black uniforms to emulate those that they supported. Pjeter Shala, who the Prosecution relies on at some point for the issue of uniforms, Pjeter Shala puts Mr. Balaj in a brown uniform or a camouflage uniform. Cars. The famous black jeep. Well, that's kind of curious because the individual who brought Sister S to the home came in a white Niva. What other objective factors do you have to rely upon? Well, his height. We don't know what it was. It was never given. It was never asked for. His weight. The colour of his hair. Any facial hair, any scars. Yes, Witness 19 testified to a scar, an old scar, a large scar. Illumination. No electricity in the home. You have no objective information concerning the description, and you have many independent pieces of evidence that give rise to doubt as to whether or not they - and by "they" I mean Witness 4 - was accurate. Now, in that regard -- and I think it's of some importance, the Prosecution's witnesses, the investigators who were involved in trying to make a determination as to who was responsible knew about and failed to follow their own guide-lines. D119 and D120. In any respect, take a look at the photo-board identification procedure report D120. I asked the following questions and noted the responses of the witness. First question: "You stated that you were a witness to certain alleged crimes. You said that you had seen a person who may be responsible. I propose to show you some photographs but before I do tell me: Have you seen that individual again in person or on television in a newspaper or other media? If so, please tell me the circumstances." Mr. Quiroz made it very clear that he was aware that there had -- this has occurred. He also made it clear that he didn't follow his own internal rules. The investigator must ascertain whether the witness has seen the suspect in a photograph or on television or on a poster. It may be that the photo-board procedure would then be inappropriate. The team legal advisor should be consulted if an identification as opposed to recognition of a witness has seen the suspect in such circumstances, and they are clearly told what recognition is, which is not what occurred here. Recognition, D119, is when the witness recognises someone from a photograph who is already known to them from some prior contact or circumstances - and I emphasise - unconnected with the alleged crime. For example, a neighbour from before the war. That's not what occurred here. They did not follow their own rules. You have no safe information upon which to feel confident at all that the individual who was involved in these series of incidents was Idriz Balaj. We know that people used Ramush's name at least on one occasion with this family. That was a lie. There are other things about what occurred, and I don't wish to fault Witness 4 at all, but the Prosecution suggested that things are absolutely true which may, in fact, not be true at all, such as whether or not the person known as Toger threatened his mother or whether or not it was, in fact, somebody else, somebody who identified specifically by name a former villager who he knew. But now going back for a moment because if you take a look at the testimony, the testimony is that they received information from Sister S that she was in Irzniq. At what period of time? Before April 22nd. Why is that important? Because April 22nd we know objectively is the day that the Serbs left Irzniq. Now, there's no dispute about the following fact, when the Black Eagles were formed, regardless of whether or not you take the date of April 14th which I think is absolutely unproved by the evidence, and I believe a review of the evidence will prove it -- will show you that, but if you take the date of April 14th, and for the moment let's accept that as the proper date, this is what occurred. On April 14th in Irzniq, 500 people got together. A clarion call was made for this group to come together. 120 were picked, and the police had not yet left Irzniq. They were still there. That did not happen. There is -- that is absolutely inconceivable. So whoever took Sister S was not a Black Eagle. Whoever was involved with that was not part of Idriz Balaj's group because the group had not yet existed, it had not been formed. That's objective evidence that you have, Your Honours. There is not overwhelming evidence of Idriz Balaj's identification. Another point which is made by the Prosecution is the issue of training and the training-ground. Now, there is evidence - and I could point out for the Court if we could pull up, it's P1217 - this is the photograph that Ylber Haskaj circled when discussing the issue of the training. And you will notice that he said that the area which is circled with a YH is the area where they trained at Gllogjan, and it has been suggested by the Prosecution that the training area was adjacent to the Ekonomija farm, and that is the language they use, adjacent to the Ekonomija farm. You will note on this photograph there is an arrow with a YH which the witness identified in his testimony in which he indicated that was the direction of the Ekonomija farm. That he does not ever remember training there, that he had no reason to train there, that he wasn't there, that he trained where he made the circle. And you can find that testimony at page 10323. The parsing of evidence, for example - and I specifically deal now with Ylber Haskaj - is -- should be of some moment to this Chamber's consideration. The Prosecution has said that Ylber Haskaj's assertion that the Black Eagles were formed on May 14th should be rejected. When Ylber Haskaj sat in that witness chair and his 92 ter statement was submitted and he testified about it and they had the opportunity to challenge that assertion, they did nothing. Now that he has left the room, and he is the only person who testified with regard to the formation of the Black Eagles in terms of being a Black Eagle and he joined the day that they were formed and he was proud of his membership, why that was not done, why the questions were not asked leaves a fair amount of question with regard to the Prosecution attempting to give to this Chamber all of the facts. I move quickly to Sanije Balaj. In order to believe that Idriz Balaj was involved, you have to believe the following. You have to believe that Avni Krasniqi is telling you the truth. He is the only person who puts Mr. Balaj there. It has been established he's a fugitive from justice from a conviction. He denied his previous convictions for robbery. He was arrested by the Office of the Prosecutor and forced to testify here. He received benefits from them, including their not informing the cooperating state of Switzerland that a person they knew was wanted was in their custody and they let him go in exchange for his testimony. In order to believe his testimony with regard to Idriz Balaj, you have to believe that he has no motivation to spin the tail spun. You must discount the testimony of Shaban Balaj, who told you they were thieves, liars, a force unto their own, a self-styled army, whose aim was to slander and rob people. You have to discount the assertions made by the Prosecution themselves that Avni was known for stopping civilians and taking cars. You have to discount the reality of the time-frame in which this incident was to have occurred. It's been pegged at the 12th. Maybe it was the 11th, perhaps not, three days later is what Mr. Avni Krasniqi says. If it was two days later, then all you have to do is take a look at D69, because that is the date the Serbs were invading Irzniq. If I suggest to you it is preposterous that the commander of the Black Eagles the day after, if you were to believe the dates, the day after toodled up to Baran, grabbed the body, and drove it back to an area and dumped it. You also have to believe what Avni Krasniqi said with regard to Sanije Balaj, that she wanted to stop and talk in the woods. You have to disbelieve his brother Mete, who told Shaban, I cannot swear for my brother because he is stained. You have to disbelieve Shaban, who said the debt has not been paid and the criminal has come out in the open. But earlier or later it will be paid, if not by brothers by someone else. You have to believe Avni Krasniqi that he is not in blood with the family, in direction contradiction to what you were told here. And you have to disbelieve a plausible alternative and, we submit, provable theory that Avni Krasniqi was involved in a robbery, that he buried Sanije Balaj in the mountains, that he got caught because there were kids who saw what happened, and that he, with others, and certainly not with Mr. Balaj, moved the body. You also have to believe something else, which is you have to believe that with regard to how the body was taken when it was removed, because do recall that he said the body was wrapped up in a blanket, he couldn't remember the colour, but it was wrapped up in a blanket, that then somebody, and that somebody would, if you believe him and you have to believe him in order to believe that Idriz Balaj was involved in this at all, unwrapped the body and put it in the two bags, because that was the state in which the body was found. In order to adopt the theory suggested by the Prosecution that the fact that she was killed because she was a collaborator, you have to discount the testimony of Cufe Krasniqi who said that he reviewed what was going on and made a determination that she was not. You have to ask yourself the serious question or the Prosecution has to answer the question what happened to the money which everybody knows was there. And finally, and most importantly: What happened to the notebook? Because the notebook is the telling evidence that she was a collaborator. The notebook is the piece of evidence that we would be given by any responsible person to deal with the issue that they suggest, that there's information in that book upon which they could rely, upon which they could make a determination of what happened and what information she had given or what contact she had; but the book went missing. There were statements made by Mr. Re yesterday that after Avni Krasniqi left Mr. Balaj, the car was driven to the canal area, but that's not what he testified to. You may recall he said he was dropped off in Bishtrica and he was asked the following question this is at 10748, this is of course -- you have to believe at this point that Toger was involved, Idriz Balaj, Toger, was involved in this whole body movement. "Which road did Toger take when he dropped you off in Bishtrica? "Well, there's a crossroad there where we were dropped off and there's a way to go to Baran and another road going to our house; however, I don't really know whether they got the direction to Gllogjan or to Baran, I don't really know that." Now, that's certainly a good example of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Re, massaging the evidence, but it also -- it also points out that, once again, if you look at all of the evidence that was presented and you look at it carefully, it doesn't add up. An evidence in a criminal case just because it's presented doesn't necessarily prove anything. It's got to be reasonable. There's got to be some logic behind what the theory is, and it doesn't exist here. And there is once again a logical reason why Avni Krasniqi is lying: Because if he admits to it, he's going to get killed. That's a pretty compelling motive, and it's real and you heard it here. You heard it from not only Shaban Balaj, but you also heard it from Avni Krasniqi. He said, I'm not in blood. I'm not in the open. I've done nothing wrong. Can you think of a more compelling reason to fabricate, to mislead? And who is -- and you heard from Rrustem Tetaj, who is Idriz Balaj? He's -- he's a stranger in the community. He's somebody who came in to -- he's somebody who came in to help fight. The easiest man to tag. He's not part of that particular community. And why not at this point dump on him? Everyone else has. Finally I wish to discuss Witness 61 and Witness 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm looking at the clock. I asked before whether you would spread evenly the time available. We had a late start, so therefore if we would not have had a late start then in two or three minutes from now you would be at half time. That means you would then have had a little bit over one hour and Mr. Harvey needs over one hour as well. So therefore, since we had a late start I suggest that we'll continue if that is agreeable with interpreters and transcribers until ten minutes past 7.00, which would also mean that in order to give you equal time that you would have another seven minutes from now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Richard. I start off with the simplest of all propositions here. Witness 61 did not identify Idriz Balaj as Toger or the man who raped her. Period. Done. Finished. Then it goes a bit further, of course. He does not fit the description of the man who raped her, and this is the second time and only the second time that we have some objective evidence with regard to the physical characteristics of that individual. She testified that he was a short, small man, just a bit taller than her, not a big man. And as the Chamber may well recall, because I was asking at that time apparently way too many questions about what she saw, how she saw, when she saw, there's no doubt that she had an opportunity to see that person. The objective evidence in this case has established she is 1.5 metres tall, translated into American that's 5 feet, 2 inches. Idriz Balaj is 1.78 metres tall. That is a substantial difference I suggest. That is not a short, small man, just a bit taller than her, not a big man. But it goes further. She told us that when she saw him on television it wasn't -- that didn't look like the man who raped her, but her family told her, her family told her that the man on television who was, in fact, Idriz Balaj, who is also known as Toger, That's Toger, that's the man who raped you. But there's no independent objective evidence of it. I won't dwell on the evidence that came from Witness 1. We have briefed that and I believe the Chamber understands our position, not having had the opportunity to cross-examine any of the information, there is -- makes it in and of itself open to question because it has not been confronted. But above and beyond that, even if you take, once again, a look at what objectively you have, Witness 1 -- and the document has been put in the Prosecution's brief, not signed, not circled, there's no -- there's no information whatsoever by looking at that particular document that as Mr. Versonnen said, the person he pointed to was that person. It's uncorroborated and you cannot rely under the teachings of Galic, you cannot rely on Versonnen's testimony to corroborate it; that's inappropriate. Above and beyond or independent of what is said with regard to the fact that any personal involvement or the failure of proof of the personal involvement of Idriz Balaj in this specific count, there is no evidence at all that has been established that the rape was carried out for the purpose of punishing or preventing suspected collaboration. I have more things to say, but recognising the time and respecting my colleague and the Chamber, I close with this. The Prosecution has failed to prove that Idriz Balaj personally committed the crimes charged against him and has utterly failed to prove that he planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of the crimes as alleged in the JCE, or joint criminal enterprise. We trust that after a careful and searing examination of the evidence, and I mean that most sincerely, a methodical, logical, scientific analysis of the evidence presented to you, that you will find Mr. Balaj not guilty of the counts that he has been charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. We will now have a break, and after the break, Mr. Harvey, it's up to you to make your closing argument, but before doing so, Mr. Emmerson, let me just ask you one tiny little question. It doesn't need any further comment if I'm right. If, however, there's any confusion I'd like to know. You referred to -- I'm talking about page 35, line 19, about the 21st of August meeting in Prapaqan about the fat fish, where from what I remember from the testimony of Witness 17 and put both in questions put by you and Mr. Kearney, reference was made to the 20th of August. I don't know whether it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Your Honour is almost certainly right and it was a slip of the tongue. I'll check my references and if I'm wrong, I'll come back to you. It's certainly the same meeting that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're wrong, we leave it as it is; if there's reason for confusion, I'd like to know. We'll have a break until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, are you ready to present your closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: More than ready, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, our closing argument, like Caesar's goal is divided into three parts. The first, the Prosecution's claim that Lahi Brahimaj was the commander of Jabllanice; the second, that he was a party to a JCE; and then finally we will deal with what conclusions we say can safely be drawn about Lahi Brahimaj and his role in the Dukagjin Zone at the material time. I will start, if I may, with a matter of law. The surprising and, we say, fatal failure by the Prosecution to move to amend the indictment on the many opportunities they have had to do so. Your Honours will recall the disparity between paragraphs 32(B) and 43 in the indictment. 32(B) alleges that Mr. Brahimaj ran a KLA detention facility at Jabllanice from "at least April until on or about the 5th of July, 1998." Paragraph 43 alleges that he ran a detention -- excuse me, that a makeshift detention facility was established in mid-May 1998 and that it was contained in a four-room house next to the family compound of Lahi Brahimaj which contained the KLA's Jabllanice headquarters. Of course the evidence was that the four-roomed house was, in fact, five or six minutes walk from the Brahimaj compound, but no matter about that at this stage. In the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, paragraph 32, they alleged that Brahimaj commanded the Jabllanice detention centre throughout the indictment period. They footnoted that, saying: "This allegation that Brahimaj commanded the Jabllanice detention centre throughout the indictment period differs from, and corrects the Prosecution's position with respect to, the allegation contained in paragraph 32 of the indictment ..." We immediately objected in our pre-trial brief filed on the 12th of February, 2007, where we put the Prosecution on notice that we opposed any attempt on the eve of trial to expand radically the case against our client since this would require additional investigation and potentially prejudice his defence. We confidently awaited a motion from the Prosecution to amend the indictment and the Court's ruling on such a motion. No motion came. We say that indictments are to be interpreted strictly. The ICTY Rules provide at Rule 50 the mechanism by which a defectively pleaded indictment can be amended, and indeed this Trial Chamber has set out in its decision of the 5th of September, 2007, the three conditions which govern its discretion to grant leave to amend. I won't go through them all, but the last of them requires that: "The proposed amendment should not result in unfair prejudice to the accused when viewed in the light of the circumstances of the case as a whole." Now, this case we are on the fourth amended indictment. The first time the indictment was amended was less than three weeks before the Prosecution filed its initial pre-trial brief, just a few days before they sought to correct with a footnote that indictment. Twice during this trial they have sought and been granted leave to amend; however, they have failed to seek leave to amend their case in relation to what we say is a crucial aspect of their case against Mr. Brahimaj. We submit that this defect cannot be cured by a mere footnote in their pre-trial brief and that they have compounded that error in paragraph [sic] 84 of their closing brief and footnote 695 [sic] thereto. More importantly, perhaps, the Prosecution has failed to provide any material to support their proposition that Lahi Brahimaj was in charge of the supposed detention facility in Jabllanice "throughout the indictment period," as they claim. Like much of their final trial brief, this claim is unsupported by evidence and is sustained merely by constant repetition, as if that were sufficient to make it so. This is not a minor point. Lahi Brahimaj has made important decisions in running his defence, not the least of which was to rely on his right not to give evidence or to call any witnesses on his behalf. He has made those decisions based on the indictment before the Court and on the evidence called by the Prosecution. To permit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- just to interrupt you. When you referred to paragraph 84, may I take it that you referred to page 84, and when you referred to footnote 695, may I take it that it could have been 697? Is that -- I put it now not to interrupt you, but otherwise if it's not on the record close to where it was said then people will miss it if later reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that correction and clarification. You caught me twice on the hop, one in that I was listening to the French to make sure that I wasn't getting ahead of myself, so I didn't hear you quite clearly; but as it finally came through, yes, you are, not for the first time, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 84. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As I was saying, Lahi Brahimaj has made these important decisions based on the indictment before the Trial Chamber and on the evidence called by the Prosecutor. To allow the Prosecution to re-interpret the indictment at this stage would result in extreme prejudice to Mr. Brahimaj. From a factual standpoint, no evidence has been presented to the Trial Chamber to suggest that anyone was detained in Jabllanice before the middle of June 1998. Again, from a factual standpoint no evidence has been presented concerning anything that happened in Jabllanice after July of 1998, with the exception of the Serb forces' attacks on the village on the 2nd and 3rd of August, 1998, that attack in which Lahi and Nazmi Brahimaj's mother and grandmother were foully and brutally murdered, and there is also of course evidence of the next attack at the beginning of September 1998. So we say as a matter of law, the Prosecution is limited to its case that Lahi Brahimaj was the alleged commander of Jabllanice beginning in May, mid-May, and ending in the first week of July 1998. Thereafter, we acknowledge the indictment alleges at paragraph 32(c) a charge that he condoned or encouraged criminal conduct by others at the alleged Jabllanice detention site, said conduct alleged to continue up until at least mid-September. While this is not supported by any facts, as a matter of law we accept that we are on notice of this allegation. That being an allegation that Lahi Brahimaj was not a commander but that he condoned mistreatment by others. We ask you to bear these legal issues in mind as we turn to the second aspect of his alleged position as commander, that's the facts, such as you may be able to rely upon them. In approaching the facts we would ask you to apply what I call the eyebrow test. Certain aspects of the Prosecution's closing argument were surprising, to say the least. One such was the claim that this case is a case of similarities. Do I hear the soft footfall of the approach of a false syllogism. Did you feel a twitch of your eyebrows at that suggestion? When the Prosecution spent seven pages of its closing argument yesterday dealing with their case against Lahi Brahimaj and their claim that he was the commander of Jabllanice, they devoted approximately one-tenth of their whole case to that claim and what they did was simply to read verbatim for six of those seven pages out of the 16 paragraphs of their closing briefs. They made no attempt to explain or expand upon those 16 paragraphs; they merely repeated to you what you have already read with care and your customary attention. I know from experience that you have read our closing briefs, and I will not be wasting your time by repeating what you already know our case to be. What are the proven facts Lahi Brahimaj and Jabllanice? Beyond the Serb forces rumour-mill, there is a disturbing lack of credible and reliable evidence about where Lahi Brahimaj was and what he was doing throughout the indictment period. You will have noted that the Prosecution appears to be downplaying its emphasis on Witness 3, and indeed as they were presenting their PowerPoint diagrams yesterday you may have noticed that they flashed a card reading: "Second abduction of Witness 3" but suddenly, and you may think wisely, they moved on without referring to it. We submit that this is because Witness 3 is an unreliable witness at best, we've dealt with this at paragraph 183 of our closing brief. He had the motive to seek the benefit of resettlement with his family, he had no fear of Lahi Brahimaj, but in his account that covered a span of a couple of months his testimony was replete with such fantastic-sounding tales of derring-do, that we wondered at times whether we weren't listening to Baron Munchausen recounting the Tales of his Marvelous Travels. With Witness 6 we have dealt with at length with his unreliability in our closing brief at paragraphs 86 to 122. And I'm only going to elaborate on certain important indications about this untruthful, evasive, and wholly unreliable witness. The eyebrow raisers begin with his claim that a police officer told him on the 30th of July, over a month before the Serb authorities claimed to have discovered remains at Lake Radoniq, and parenthetically we take on board everything that Mr. Emmerson said about the fabrications that occurred at that stage, but he claimed that on the 30th of July he was told that Nenad Remistar's body was not dumped in the lake as many others, but may be buried in the mountains, that's transcript 5312. We say this gives strong support to our contention that he is deliberately lying and embellishing his story out of his own hatred for the Brahimajs. His answers about his relationships to the head of the RDB in Gjakove were, to say the least, far from frank and satisfactory. The idea that he would have had a chance meeting in the coffee shop of the Hotel Pashtrik during the very time the Serbian forces were planning to launch a massive attack against Jabllanice and that Sreten Camovic would simply ask him, Well, how were things in Jabllanice, that idea does not survive the eyebrow test or any other. We have to ask: Can we dismiss from our minds and, with respect, can you dismiss from yours the strong suspicion that this man's testimony has already been bought and paid for by his masters in Jagodina that he goes at such lengths to visit and that he is and perhaps was at all times an agent of the Serbian forces himself? How else to explain his claim that even after he says he was free to leave Jabllanice he decided not to go, but instead to stick around and find out what he could about people? Why? He had clearly as he came into this courtroom a motive of revenge. He had been humiliated by being accused of the crime of collaboration and of having carried an unauthorised pistol, both pistol and his suspiciously expensive car were confiscated at Jabllanice. He had a motive of revenge and he articulated it in the most clear fashion when he said that, I told Nazmi Brahimaj: There will be bloodshed because of this car. This is not the statement of a frightened man. We say this was a declaration of blood-feud against the Brahimaj family. They must be made to pay for taking his car, and he came to this court to make them pay. His obsession on this point was emphasised by his asking you, the Trial Chamber, at the conclusion of his testimony, Would you please give him compensation or tell him how he could get compensation for his car. Is this a witness on whom you can really rely beyond a reasonable doubt? We say no and we say there is a need with a witness of this kind to look for corroboration; there is none, we say. We have to ask. Even in relation to his claims of his serious injuries, was he beaten at all by anyone? If he was, it surely cannot have been of the frequency or severity which he claimed because the injuries would have been devastating. Can we believe that Lahi Brahimaj encouraged or condoned any such ill-treatment. Did he really sustain any fracture at all, as he claimed? If he did, it's most surprising perhaps that the OTP's investigators never looked for the X-ray that he was supposed to have taken home with him which now mysteriously it cannot be found. We asked on the 12th of November for that X-ray to be sought and produced; we're still waiting. As between Witness 3 and Witness 6, there are several irreconcilable conflicts of which again we will highlight one or two. Witness 3 claims that he was in the barracks for three days and two nights; Witness 6 says Witness 3 was there for a matter of hours. Witness 6 says there was only one person there from Grabanice who on the evidence before us must presumably have been Witness 3, but Witness 6 says this man was not beaten or even touched. Why? Because his wife came from Jabllanice. Witness 6 says that Nazmi and Hamz beat Pal Krasniqi. Witness 3 says, no, it was Naser, otherwise known as Rusi. Witness 6 says two people sought to escape from the alleged detention centre; Witness 3 says, no, there was only one who tried to escape and that was Skender Kuci. The evidence about what was happening in Jabllanice is tenuous and far from satisfactory, but the evidence of Lahi Brahimaj being the commander there simply does not exist we say. Probably the strongest element that the Prosecution has to introduce in that regard comes from Jakup Krasniqi who -- and I just refer Your Honours to page 5010 of the transcript, was asked at some length about this and what he said ultimately was: "He was the person that I knew," within the Dukagjin Zone and the "person I communicated with. I think he was responsible for the area at that time." What does this mean? Is this evidence that Lahi Brahimaj was in fact an officer commanding soldiers in the Dukagjini Zone or even in Jabllanice itself? We say the realistic and common-sense view must be that as Jakup Krasniqi said, the two of them, he and Lahi, were working together at that time in the Berisha mountains. Krasniqi knew that Lahi was from that area, and if he needed to know anything about the terrain or the people in the area, of course he's going to talk to the man who is working right next to him. In June there is no evidence that Jakup Krasniqi had any contact inside Dukagjin. The only person he had available was the man he said was frequently there with him in the Berisha mountains, Lahi Brahimaj. He also said that he himself visited the barracks in Jabllanice, but he saw no evidence that there was any kind of prison there. There are two exhibits which shed some light on the extent to which we can be confident that Lahi Brahimaj was not exercising command responsibility in the region, but that he had other far different responsibilities. At the beginning of June, the 8th of June, and I don't ask for it to be called up, I simply refer to Exhibit P126 and to page 7 of the English translation of that, where reference is made to Dushkaja being under pressure, Dushkaja being the region in which Jabllanice finds itself. A new front and a need for officers/commanders and flour. A need for officers or commanders. Not a suggestion that Lahi Brahimaj has got it all under his control. Don't worry, that's Lahi's area. Exhibit P206 takes us to the 15th of July and a complaint made by Lahi Brahimaj about being treated very roughly by guards in Gllogjan, ironically on a street called Jabllanice Street, while he was accompanying a group that had come from Albania and were on their way to Dashinoc. If he was so well-known, if he was a commander, would any soldier have treated him in this fashion? And would he have had to raise it repeatedly as that exhibit indicates that he did and even to have to reduce it to writing? To the extent that the Prosecution case relies on rumours and hearsay, then let them also explain why Witness 38 reported that she heard that the commander of Jabllanice had a long white beard. I come to the second main aspect of our submissions, and that is concerns the alleged JCE. And in doing so, I know it has not escaped your attention that the goal-posts have shifted. They have shifted from an allegation that the purpose of the JCE was to secure control of the zone to an allegation that its purpose was the ethnic cleansing of Serbs within that zone, for which there is no reliable, credible evidence, no evidence of that going on in Jabllanice. Certainly it was the goal of those in Jabllanice, of those in the KLA, of all of those struggling for the independence of Kosovo to ensure control of the zone, but not by despicable means. Just as Mr. Emmerson has indicated the reasons why there was no reason for Mr. Haradinaj to be -- to know or to suspect anything being amiss in Jabllanice, because he was not there except on very rare occasions, there is no proof that Lahi Brahimaj was there except on very rare occasions, specifically two occasions about which you have heard, one towards the end of May when Fadil Fazliu puts him there, that's not challenged, and one for about three days before the 19th of July. Why do I say that? Because Bislim Zyrapi travelled from the Berisha Mountains in company with Lahi Brahimaj, who of course was working in the General Staff headquarters with him. They travelled in the middle of July to Jabllanice first, they had a meeting there, following which Mr. Zyrapi went to visit Gllogjan and a number of other locations. The testimony suggests that he was gone for about two, perhaps three days, and then urgently was recalled to Jabllanice where Lahi Brahimaj was waiting for him with orders to take him to Rahovec where a Serb attack was underway. So we have Lahi in Jabllanice for two to three days ending on the 19th of July. Again, the fact that his job was to take Bislim Zyrapi to Rahovec indicates further that his duties were those of a staff officer on the General Staff rather than a command officer at Jabllanice, because if there's a Serb attack going on the commander of Jabllanice would need to stay in Jabllanice. Apart from this there is no proof that rises to the level of beyond a reasonable doubt that Lahi Brahimaj was in Jabllanice at the time when Skender Kuci is alleged to have been brought there. The Trial Chamber does not have a precise date for the alleged abduction of Skender Kuci. It is not clear of course whether Mr. Kuci was abducted by Serbs initially and possibly mistreated by them prior to going to Jabllanice. Assuming that Witness 6 is at least partially reliable and truthful about this, it is still impossible to put a date on the arrival of the man from Zahaq who he described coming to Jabllanice in the boot of a car. He puts it as a week or two before he was released. Does this constitute proof beyond a reasonable doubt that Lahi Brahimaj must have been there at that time? Certainly not. Similarly in relation to Pal Krasniqi, we lack proof beyond a reasonable doubt that Lahi Brahimaj was there at the time when he was allegedly detained. The evidence there is that according to Ded Krasniqi, Mahir Demaj and Pal Krasniqi left their home on about the 10th of July, they were beaten up by Serbs that night, and could not have arrived in Jabllanice earlier than the 11th. We don't know whether it may have been later. We do know according to Mahir Demaj's 92 bis statement that they were taken to an improvised hospital in Jabllanice to recover from their beatings at the hands of the Serb police. Again Mahir Demaj indicates they were given uniforms five days after their arrival. So we don't have a precise date for the time when allegedly there was suspicion that Pal Krasniqi might be an informant or a collaborator. And parenthetically I should also add that the claim that Pal Krasniqi was shot at the canal wall is again supposition. It cannot be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. It is known forensically that he had been shot and killed sometime prior to that and his body brought there at a later stage. It is impossible to rule out the strong likelihood that this man who was still walking around, recovering from his injuries according to Witness 6, if he is to be believed, as of the 25th of July it is impossible to rule out the strong possibility that he was still in Jabllanice when the Serbs attacked on the 2nd and 3rd of August. It is impossible to rule out the doubt as to the cause of his death being Serbs attacking, taking him prisoner, or killing him on the spot and then disposing of him at their pleasure. In relation to the office, so-called, that was supposed to be Lahi Brahimaj's room in the barracks at Jabllanice, again the Prosecution claim that he was still responsible for Jabllanice because he maintained an office there. This is -- really does not pass the laugh test let alone the eyebrow test. Pjeter Shala said that soldiers slept in a kind of office, a so-called office, because it only had a desk inside, nothing else, and his description is at pages 9951 to 9953 of the transcript. In the entire claim that Lahi Brahimaj was in command of Jabllanice rests on what we say is an ahistorical or anti-historical approach by the Prosecution. What they have done is to take a few snatches of Serb intelligence information, collate it together during 1995 to 1997, to that mixture they have added bits and pieces from all over the place and at all kinds of different epochs or periods during 1997 to 1998, irrespective of whether they fall before, during, or after the indictment period. They have thrown this into a stew, they have turned up the heat, and they have stirred it around. This is not a basis on which this Tribunal can rely for determining what Lahi Brahimaj's role was. The Prosecution goes further. They say this is a case of similarities, rather than one in which each and every one of their contentions must be tested by the required standard of proof before it can be considered in relation to their other claims. The step-by-step approach advocated by Mr. Emmerson is, we say, the only proper approach, and I'm sure it is the one that Your Honours are going to take. The claim that Lahi Brahimaj was in control at Jabllanice at any time, let alone throughout the indictment period, appears to be based primarily on the claim that he had an office or a room in the makeshift barracks. It is a pathetic allegation. There are many accounts given by many witnesses, and as Mr. Guy-Smith has, we believe, very rightly pointed out, many of these witnesses have given their statements years, many years, after the events to which they relate. This is not a case in which an examining magistrate has carefully taken sworn statements, and a number of the original statements you have watched fall apart before your eyes as witnesses have come into this room and have failed to come up to the proof contained in those statements, particularly when it's come to issues of identification and important detail. And there is one particular witness statement which has been admitted, not tested by cross-examination for obvious reasons, and that's P1248, the 92 quater statement of the father of Witness 6. We say that statement is not capable of providing corroboration of any kind for Witness 6's claims against Lahi Brahimaj, not least because the maker of that statement -- excuse me, let me rephrase that. Not least because Witness 6 was present in the room at the time that that statement was being taken and in a strong position to influence its contents. In our brief at paragraph 173, I just draw attention to this, we have referred to the strong doubts that must exist about Pjeter Shala's claim that the military police were formed as early as March of 1998. That cannot be the case if, as he claims, Hashim Thaqi was involved in recommending him to become a member of the military police. I apologise, I said that this was referred to in our brief at paragraph 173; I'm referring of course to the Prosecution's brief at paragraph 173, which make this, in our view, totally erroneous claim. We also draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to paragraph 617 of the Prosecution brief relating to Pal Krasniqi's remains and the conclusions that can really safely be drawn from that finding. And we note the use of the word "probably" by the Prosecution which is a clear red light to any finder of fact that this is not something that can possibly be relied on for the proposition which they seek to advance there. The cornerstone of our argument, Your Honours, is that we ask you quite simply to take a common-sense approach. What do you think is really the situation that operated in the zone at the time, in Jabllanice at the time, given the conditions that the KLA in its nascent stage was seeking to operate under, constantly harassed, constantly attacked, constantly in danger of interception and being killed. At this stage in history we all have some sense of how national liberation movements develop, seeing the struggle, the victorious struggle of the ANC in South Africa. We know that Nelson Mandela started out with a very small group of individuals who went away to get a different kind of training from the lawyers that they had initially thought they were going to remain. They went to get military training. They went back inside the country and they started to stir things up. They started with sabotage attacks, they started with attacks on police installations, and they were very soon caught and sentenced. Others took their place. Gradually they made advances in one area, losing ground again, constantly having to react to the enemy's tactics. Umkhonto we Sizwe was founded in 1960, the armed wing of the ANC. It took them 30 years to approach victory when Mandela was finally released in 1990. It took another four years to take power. The speed with which the KLA grew was quite a bit fast than that, but the chaos which surrounded it and the growing pains that it went through are a matter, just as I suggest, of common sense that we can all recognise. This was not simply a straight-line process, as the Prosecution seem to want you to believe. All we ask you to do is to consider what is the likely situation for Lahi Brahimaj? When people refer to him as having been a commander or the commander in Jabllanice, you look at all of the references to that that are advanced by witnesses such as Zoran Stijovic and they all rely on sources from 1996, 1997, and the very latest is February of 1998. We do not dissent from the suggestion that Lahi Brahimaj was a prominent and the most prominent figure in Jabllanice at that time, but circumstances change. Ramush Haradinaj comes into the country around that time, Nazmi Brahimaj returns to the country around that time, and at that stage the struggle begins to take on a different complexion. Later on other leaders enter the country, and most importantly towards the end of May you have Bislim Zyrapi and Hashim Thaqi arriving, and what is then the most important focus? It is consolidating and forming the General Staff inside the country because once again common sense tells us and witnesses have told us that there was discontent in the movement inside the country about these so-called leaders who were outside, in Albania or elsewhere. Bislim Zyrapi recognised that was why it was important for them to enter the country and to take the struggle to a new level. In taking the struggle to a new level, they need more than anything the assistance of one of the very few General Staff members who had remained in the country, Lahi Brahimaj. They don't need him to be stranded in Jabllanice; they need him to be in the Berisha Mountains with them consolidating the General Staff. And what were his responsibilities? His responsibilities were organizing supply routes, as is hinted at by the complaint we already referred to at P206; and his responsibilities were the finances of the KLA. Now, one thing you do not do if you are running an organization of that nature is have your finance officer charging off all around the place and running a completely separate operation from the General Staff. Common sense tells us again that what Colonel Crosland told this Trial Chamber is absolutely reliable and correct. This whole indictment period constituted a fluid situation, and you would not expect a fledgling national liberation struggle to be operating in a static fashion. Once new commanders have taken over in one area, for instance, Nazmi, as we know, in Jabllanice, there is no need for Lahi to remain there. He has skills and experience that are too important to be wasted anywhere but being in the General Staff. He is not anywhere around the area of Lake Radoniq. He is not in Jabllanice. His job is not to command soldiers in the field, it is not to deal with individuals suspected of collaboration. None of these are his concern. His knowledge of the supply routes from Albania that he's been running for months, if not years, according to those Serb intelligence documents upon which the Prosecution places so much reliance, that knowledge is vital for the General Staff as it moves to consolidate its struggle at a life-or-death moment for the liberation of Kosovo. That is what you would expect and that is what we submit was happening. It is not for us to prove any aspect of that. We have stood on our client's right to put the Prosecution to the strict proof of its case. We put them to that proof and we say they have failed in every respect. We submit that our client should be found gui -- brilliant. No, not coupable. We submit of course that our client should be found not guilty on each and every count that he faces. I thank Your Honours for your attention throughout this trial.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. We -- it's no use, Mr. Re, to invite you to start to make further submissions, so we'll adjourn for the day. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, the 23rd of January, quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom, where you then, Mr. Re, will have one hour; and Defence counsel together will have one hour and a half for rebuttal and rejoinder. And then finally if the Chamber has any additional questions there will be time available to put them to counsel. We stand adjourned.
